sweep_summary: Two title-hits for jama1261 (Madi; both actually about the Banawá variety, bana1307). (1) Buller, Buller & Everett 1993 (IJAL 59(3):280-293, DOI 10.1086/466199): open author copy on daneverettbooks. it is the original first-hand description that the catalog's current deciding source (Everett 1996 ROA-121) restates, and it confirms the weight coding (CV/CVV only, one mora per vowel, stress every other vowel L->R within the word, initial vowel extraprosodic except in bimoraic words, tautosyllabic vowels may belong to different feet) while adding, in n. 5, the hedged primary-stress rule (penultimate stress-bearing vowel, 'numerous exceptions') that Everett 1996 lacks in prose; recommended as the citation of record, with Everett 1996 kept for the degenerate-foot and diphthong-weight detail. (2) Wiltshire 2004, MA thesis (University of Manchester, 71 pp.) on stress in connected speech in Banawá: no online copy found (Glottolog record has no URL; Manchester Library Search returns 0 local hits for it; medium acquisition priority (first-hand, but phrase-level, and unlikely to displace BBE 1993). all look-ups were done with direct download/automated download. Saved files and are under Manchester Library Search also surfaced two theoretical reanalyses of the BBE data not in the item list (Hyde, 'Issues in Banawá Prosody', LI; Martínez-Paricio & Kager, LI note on Banawá grid vs. metrical structure), not downloaded.

new_statements.reading: Banawá (Madi) has iterative left-to-right binary left-headed (trochaic) feet built over vowels/moras within the grammatical word: every odd-numbered nucleus from the left is stressed, a word-initial vowel is extraprosodic (unstressed) in words of more than two vowels but stressed in bimoraic words (minimality), syllables are CV or CVV with one mora per vowel and feet may split a CVV syllable. Primary stress is only tentatively assigned (footnote): generally the penultimate stress-bearing vowel, with many exceptions. This is the peer-reviewed, first-hand description by the resident fieldworkers (the Bullers, ~six years with the Banawá; 1989 SIL corpus) that Everett 1996 restates; it confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding (CVV = two moras, mora-counting trochees) and supplies the primary-stress statement the current deciding source lacks in prose.

audit.recode_to: No change to kind. Fill the primary-stress field: 'primary stress on the penultimate stressed vowel (rightmost non-final foot head); never on the word-final mora' from held BBE 1993 fn.5 p.288 and MP&K 2020 pp.169,173 (edge: right-oriented main stress over L-to-R alternating count). Add a caution that the system counts vowels/moras and splits CVV syllables, so some analysts (MP&K 2020:169) label it 'quantity-insensitive rhythmic stress on alternating vowels'; CVV counts as two positions, which is what the 'weight / CVV' coding encodes.

sources.note: Silent on stress. The work describes Jarawara, which Vogel treats as a sister dialect of Banawá within Madi, not Banawá itself; the even/odd mora-parity alternation in the phonological word is compatible with (and indirectly supports) the left-to-right mora-counting trochaic analysis in the existing Buller, Buller & Everett 1993 statement but says nothing about stress placement.
